utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning again to everybody. I can't count the days with this witness, but I think again we have witness Nicolai and he should be brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And Mr. President, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning to you and Your Honours. Good morning, General Tolimir, Mr. Gajic. Good morning, everyone. I just wanted to let the Court know that the Prosecution is prepared to respond orally if the Court wishes to devote a little time at the end of one of the sessions to addressing both the issues of the intercept operator about whom we spoke yesterday, with the Rule 70 issue, as well as the pending motion to add or convert two other intercept operators who are currently on the schedule. We've received responses from the accused on both counts. I'm prepared to address both orally to save time and expedite the proceedings if the Court so desires at any time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The Chamber has not received yet application by Mr. Tolimir about the witness concerned, the intercept operator, but we are looking forward to your application. I haven't seen anything yet. Have you sent something to the Chamber? Okay. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in the course of yesterday, we did send a copy of that request linked to protective measures. We provided it to the Registrar, to Mr. Thayer, and the court assistants, and it was officially filed and registered today. I think it will be registered in a couple of minutes time actually just now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, thank you very much. I was informed that indeed we received, as agreed yesterday, an e-mail and we will deal with this very fast and during today, I think. But I'm not very optimistic and it's not very likely that this witness we are talking about will be in the position to testify this week. We have some doubt that this is possible. Nevertheless, we should start with the current witness. Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Welcome again to the Tribunal, and again, let me tell you the affirmation to tell the truth still applies. And Mr. Tolimir has some more questions for you. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I'd like to greet all those present and may peace reign in this house. And may God's will be done and not necessarily my own will. I'd like to say good morning to General Nicolai and to welcome him amongst us once again. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, General, we were discussing freedom of movements yesterday -- freedom of movement yesterday, and the Bandera Triangle and the Muslim forces did not allow your forces to move around. Now, I'm going to show you a map so that you can see where the general area is. But first of all, I'm going to tell you what General Franken said at this trial so you can bear that that mind and then we can hear your opinion. It's the transcript of the 30th of June, 2010, page 3383, lines 21 to 24. He was speaking about the so-called Bandera Triangle and Mr. Franken said the following, and I quote: "It was an area where we did not have freedom of movement. We attempted to establish a regime in the sector but when we tried to do that, the United Nations withdrew their order and said all right, let that go." Now on the 1st of July transcript, 2010, on page 3410 and 3411, we see mention of negotiations and Colonel Franken was not a participant in the negotiations, but he said: "During those negotiations, the UN withdrew the order for establishing freedom of movement." Now, in response to a question that he was asked, what he understands by the United Nations --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker kindly slow down, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: -- he referred to the higher echelons. And I'll try and explain that. Sarajevo --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you are too fast again. The interpreters can't catch what you are saying.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I apologise to the interpreters. I'll bear that in mind. I'll try and slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now in response to the question of what he understood that the United Nations meant, in 3411, Colonel Franken said: "I would like to refer you to the higher echelons and I'll try to explain this. In that case, Sarajevo became involved directly and it is customary that our superior echelons be the north-east sector, although Sarajevo usually took on the role of making decisions." I'll stop there because I see that Mr. Thayer is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed, and Mr. Tolimir, if you see the space on the record, you see there's no question yet, it is a very long statement and a report about another witness. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, it just might help the witness, particularly the interpreters, and I think everybody if we just, like we did yesterday, put the portion of the transcript on e-court so everybody can follow along. I think it will just help the proceedings if we could do that again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed, that would be very helpful. I think, Mr. Tolimir, you are quoting from different parts of the transcript. Can you call up, please, the relevant part so that the witness can see what the other witness, Colonel Franken, told the Court.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I've said what he stated but it is the 1st of July -- or rather, the 30th of June transcript, 2010. Page 3383, lines 21 to 24. So may that be called up on e-court so that we can all take a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: If you've had a chance to look at the transcript there, the next transcript page on the 1st of July --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We've just received the transcript. You can see it as well. Give the appropriate time for the witness and wait a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I think the Defence will agree the relevant portion begins a little further up on page 3382. In fact, that may have been where General Tolimir was quoting, but I think the relevant portion starts a little bit up there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Which line, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Beginning about line 12 is where the Bandera Triangle portion begins, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Have you had a chance to read through that portion, General? Yes?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Take a look at the transcript of the 1st of July, 2010, and the page there is 3410 and 3411. And reference is made to negotiations between the United Nations and the BH Army. And I just quoted one sentence from that portion. 3411, lines 9 to 13. That's where I was quoting from. Please tell us when you finish looking through it.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, may we have on e-court D65, which is a map, so that the General can see the area this refers to where freedom of movement was banned. D65, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: While we are waiting for that to come up, I'm going to ask the General the following: Did you receive the information, General, about the enclave from two sources, directly from DutchBat and the sector whose headquarters were in Tuzla? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ordinarily we received all information regarding the sector from the Tuzla headquarters, the north-east sector, but as I've said previously, sometimes I was in direct contact with Colonel Karremans, but not about this matter. I'd like to make that clear from the outset.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. You can see the map now and the triangle is in blue with the numbers 1, 2, and 3, and the arrows that was drawn in by Colonel Franken in his own hand. So that's the zone while you were in authority there, UNPROFOR forces were not allowed to move around. Do you see that? Do we need to zoom in?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is as follows: Since the sector issued the order to establish a check-point here at number 1, as indicated by the Colonel, and when the Muslims forbid that, was it customary for your command, superior command, to have been informed about the activities of units in the area, in the sector? Would you have had to have known about that and been informed about it? The UNPROFOR command in Sarajevo, I mean.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think so. If their operations were being impeded, they undoubtedly would have reported that, but I assume that this took place before I arrived in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. It took place before you arrived, that's true, but it went on while you were there, your forces were not allowed to move around in that triangle. And the order came, as Colonel Franken said, from Sarajevo that UNPROFOR forces should not be given freedom of movement in that area. Now my question this: If the UNPROFOR forces controlled the demilitarised zone in Srebrenica, then the agreement we saw yesterday, did it allow freedom of movement in the zone? Thank you. And we read out the conditions in that agreement.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, I'm not aware of any restrictions on freedom of movement, let alone that that order was issued from Sarajevo. In any case, that did not happen during my term as Chief of Staff. Conceivably that might have happened earlier, but then it's strange that my predecessor didn't notify me about that. If such a restriction on freedom of movement did apply, then I would imagine that it wasn't reiterated when I was Chief of Staff and I assume that in practice during that period, it wasn't really such an issue because, as already mentioned, there was a serious fuel shortage and the only possible way of patrolling was on foot. So in practice, that restriction on freedom of movement won't really have been such a problem in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I have understood you. This was the activity that Colonel Franken testified about and he said that they didn't dare move around because that was the order issued by Sarajevo. So I put that to you now and I put to you the passage in the transcript and his testimony, so what can you tell us about that? Or rather, did higher echelons have the right to restrict UNPROFOR, its movements, following a request from the side that they are, in fact, controlling, in this case, it was the Muslim side? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course, a higher echelon can impose restrictions, but the question is whether it's wise to do so. To me it's inconceivable. Yesterday, I already said that freedom of movement is essential for a peacekeeping mission to perform its duties. I can hardly imagine them issuing instructions to impose restrictions. In any case, I was not informed in any way at all about that and I can't say anything else about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now, Colonel Franken said here that there was an order from the north-east sector on the restriction of movement in this Bandera Triangle that we see on the map. Now, can you explain to us whether you as the command of the sector were duty-bound, or your predecessors, to inform the command of Sector North-east that you went against their order to establish freedom of movement in the Bandera Triangle? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I had been aware of those restrictions on freedom of movement, then I certainly would have investigated the reason for them and would have discussed this with the north-east sector and have tried to reverse that. But I repeat once again that I had no idea whatsoever about this and it still surprises me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General, I understand. But tell me this: This situation, was that the situation when you were the chief as well?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean by "this situation"?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was it forbidden for UN soldiers to move around the triangle marked 1, 2, and 3, throughout 1995 until the very end, until they stayed in Srebrenica and while you were on duty there? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I think this question is a problem because the witness said he doesn't know anything about these restrictions in the Bandera Triangle. How can he say something about the existence of this triangle during his period of service?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you, Mr. President. But that's why I showed the General statements and documents where his subordinates speak about this situation. So if he didn't know about it before, he knows about it now, so I'm asking him what he thinks about this, whether it's customary, the usual thing, and whether it was still on-going while he was on duty there. Whether that was the situation while he took up his post.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: These are two different questions. The first one is a new one and the second one is -- you asked him already but he can't answer this question. You have got everything you can get from this witness about this point. You should carry on but not insist on this point. If the witness says, "I was not aware of the situation," how can he say anything about that further? You should carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I'm asking about this situation, the phenomenon. And may we now have 1D240 called up, please. It's a report from the command of the 28th Division, dated the 29th of April, 1995, sent to the 2nd Corps command. And this was the period when the General was on duty there. Thank you. Since there's no English translation, I'm going to read it and I'm going to read the second paragraph which starts with "1000 hours ..." You can see the numbers, "At 1000 hours ..." And we are talking about the 24th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: "At 1000 hours," it says, "on the same day," that is to say, the 29th of April, that's my comment, "a meeting was held of the representatives of the command of the 28th Division and organs of the civilian authorities with representatives of the United Nations liaison officers and military observers. At the meeting" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please slow down again because there's no English translation. It's very difficult for the interpreters. Very slow, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Let me repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This event took place and the 29th of April, and I'm reading from paragraph 2. "At 1000 hours" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, Mr. Tolimir, this is on the record already. Starts with the words: "At the meeting ..."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Everything is fine up to that point.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: "At the meeting, the participants discussed problems linked to the establishment of an observation post in the locality of Lozina and our position was presented in conformity with your order. The United Nations representatives attending the meeting took the position that as far as that observation post was concerned, they should install it because they had an order to do that from their superior command. And they explained that it was been their mandate and it was used by both sides and that it would serve the exclusive interests of the enclave." Now I'd like to read paragraph 4 and it begins with the following: "Our side -- our side insisted that the UN representatives unconditionally cease further engineering on construction work of this observation post and that they should withdraw from that location, withdraw all their men until a solution to the problem is found. Our proposal was fully supported by the head of the military observers, Mr. Romilton from Brazil, while the UN liaison officer resolutely accepted the proposal, or rather, he agreed that he stop further construction of the observation post and to keep the people there using the location for observation until a suitable solution is found." So from what I've just read out from this document, we can see that the problem was an on-going one and it lasted, in fact, for four months and that construction work was under way during that time. So resources had to be set aside for this, and funds, so there must have been an order about this. So should the command in Sarajevo have known about it -- this and is it possible that it wasn't receiving information from this sector for four months while you were on duty there as well? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that should be clear from the fact that this is the first I hear of it. Undoubtedly, the north-east sector was involved, but in Sarajevo I never heard anything about this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go back to the first paragraph, I need it in order to be able to put another question to the General.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The first paragraph is here in front of you and I'm going to read the first sentence. "You sent us a document under the following number and date in which you sent us an order to stop the construction works on the observation post of the United Nations in the Lozina village sector." And now could you please answer my question. Do you know that there was a corridor between the demilitarised zone of Zepa and Srebrenica? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of the existence of such a corridor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Do you know that there was a meeting, referred to in this document, on the 29th of April, and were you informed about the discussions that took place during that meeting?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of that, but please understand that there were dozens of battalions that all had their local discussions with the authorities, so it wasn't possible to notify the headquarters in Sarajevo about all those meetings' discussions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Could you kindly explain what you meant. We are talking about the restriction of movements through a zone that UNPROFOR was supposed to supervise.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you please be more specific in your question because at this point it's so general that I can't respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I will rephrase my question. The Bandera area that we saw on the map is within the demilitarised zone of Srebrenica. According to the agreement on the demilitarisation, the United Nations were duty-bound to control whether that agreement was implemented and that's why they had to have freedom of movements across the entire zone. Was it customary for the command of UNPROFOR in Sarajevo not to be informed that all of a sudden the movement of troops was restricted in a certain part of the zone, in this case two villages, one of them being the village of Lozina and the other the village of Suceska? Thank you. There are several villages, as a matter of fact. You saw the map and you saw how many villages there were in that demilitarised zone.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: With all due respect, General Tolimir, I am aware that I already answered this question. I think it's highly unusual for an area that was under UNPROFOR control, there would have been restriction on freedom of movement for UNPROFOR, and if I had known about this, I certainly would have objected. But I'm saying now for the last time, I was not aware of this so I cannot elaborate any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. And what about your previous answer, what did you mean when you said that there were a lot of battalions there? Did you mean the battalions within the Muslim armed formations or, rather, battalions within the framework of UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, of course, I was referring to the UNPROFOR structure. We had three sectors and there were several battalions that reported to each sector, so obviously not all those battalions reported to Sarajevo exactly what they discussed with the local authorities. It was only if there was a serious problem that could be resolved only at the highest echelons that something like that would be reported, and otherwise, those people solved their own problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Colonel Franken testified here and said that the issue was referred to the superior command in Sarajevo, but let me ask you this: You saw that there was reference to Mr. Romilton who accepted that there wouldn't be patrols in the area. This person, Romilton, did he belong to a different structure? Did he report to a different structure or was he duty-bound to abide by UNPROFOR's guide-lines and was he duty-bound to report to the UNPROFOR command? We are talking about the head of military observers, Mr. Romilton from Brazil. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If Mr. Romilton was the head of the military observers in Srebrenica, then he had to report to the head of the UNMO sector of the north-east sector headquarters in Tuzla, which in turn reported to the head of the UNMO sector in Sarajevo. Of course, intensive consultation took place between the UNMOs and the rest of UNPROFOR despite the absence of a direct command relationship, but I can't imagine that the UNMOs would have gone against the UNPROFOR policy by accepting restrictions on freedom of movement. And had that been the case, then in any case, I am particularly unhappy about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Was my quotation correct or are you saying that this didn't happen at all, that Romilton didn't accept things as it is stated herein? Are you saying that what I read out does not reflect the situation on the ground?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't allege that because I have no knowledge of this matter, so I can't allege that it didn't happen. So I'm not questioning your allegations, all I'm saying is that if it happened, then I deeply regret that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the document please be admitted into evidence and the document is 1D246, the one that we quoted from that was on the screen. Could it please be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is that really 1D246 or 1D40?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: It's 1D240, Mr. President. Sorry, I spoke before being recognised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just for the record, per our usual policy, we have no objection to the admission of the document, recognising, of course, that this witness repeatedly has stated that he has no familiarity with the underlying circumstances, much less the document itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This document will be marked for identification. In this case, not pending translation, but because this witness was not able to identify the authenticity of the content.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 1D240 will be Exhibit D82, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would kindly ask you to allow me to say a sentence. I want things to be evidence of events and phenomena. It doesn't really matter whether the witness was an eye-witness to the events. He was on duty, and the previous evidence prove that there were violations in the demilitarised zone and that UNPROFOR was prevented from performing their duty in a corridor, in a zone. And this is why I tendered the document into evidence. We had a witness who testified here who was a participant in the events. He told us what had happened and he told us that he had delegated the matter to the command in Sarajevo, and that's why I asked this witness about the entire matter because the problem prevailed for almost a year. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, this was a very long sentence indeed, but I see your point. There are different ways to tender documents. One is through a witness, but this is the wrong witness. Perhaps there will be another witness, the Chamber doesn't know that, and there's a possibility to move for admission of documents from the bar table. That could happen as well, but it's up to you which way you are choosing. In this case today, it is not possible to admit this document into evidence. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Could the court please produce 1D242. Thank you. We have it on the screen now. Again there's no English translation. The order was issued on the 29th April 1995, which means that the witness was on duty at the time when this order was issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I will read from bullet point 2 since there's no translation. And I quote: "In our contacts with the representatives of the Dutch Battalion, we should strictly adhere by the position that the distribution of observation points has been agreed in the agreement on the demilitarisation of Srebrenica and Zepa at the level of the Main Staff of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the UNPROFOR command for Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that any change has to be confirmed in the same way and at the same level. Every change has to be confirmed by the same level." I said "in the same way" and I misspoke. I apologise. End of quotation. My question to you, sir, is this: Do you know anything about this event that happened in the month of April? Do you know anything about the fact that the commands of the BiH Army and the command of the UNPROFOR in Bosnia-Herzegovina had agreed as to how the observation points would be distributed and how control would be implemented in the demilitarised zones? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't have the English translation, so I can't speak with any authority on this, but just from what I understand from LiveNote, that's not what this document purports to state, that there was any agreement between the General Staff of the army and UNPROFOR. In fact, I think it reflects the opposite, that the General Staff of the ABiH was telling its subordinate command to adhere to the prior demilitarisation agreement and that there was no agreement about the new observation post that the UN was trying to impose in this area. Again, I don't have the English but that sounded to me like an incorrect recitation of what General Tolimir himself quoted from the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, the Chamber would prefer to hear this answer from the witness himself. Mr. Nicolai, could you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The locations of the observation posts as they were when I entered my position were the same as when the enclave was taken into use over one year earlier. I'm not aware of which agreements were reached at that time, but one thing is beyond any doubt, during my term no proposals were made to set up new observation posts. So everything in this document is news to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Do you know if ever at the level of UNPROFOR forces in Srebrenica and the command of the BiH Army there were agreements about the deployment of UNPROFOR forces and was their movement restricted in any way by those agreements?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my previous answer I just stated that I'm not aware of agreements made about this and that answer still applies.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. And can you now answer the following question: Yesterday you saw an agreement, the agreement on the demilitarisation of Zepa and Srebrenica. According to that agreement, were the BiH Army command forces those that determined the locations of the UNPROFOR observation posts within the demilitarised zone? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that seems exceptionally unlikely to me, but I can't remember reading that in any agreement yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. That means that the BiH Army could not determine those locations, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know, the BiH certainly did not determine that. It's possible that consultations took place about that, but I can't imagine that they determined that. That sounds particularly strange that one of the parties concerned would have the final say in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. My next question is this: Did you personally control the Sector North as a superior command and the communication with the Dutch Battalion, and did you inquire with Karremans about the presence of the BiH Army and its activities within the demilitarised zone?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Sector North-east.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this question is so general that it's particularly difficult to answer. If there was a report about activities of the BiH Army in the demilitarised zone, then I may very well have asked a question about that at some point. But if you can't be more specific about what you mean, then there's little point to that answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I'll try and be more specific in my question. When it comes to the Dutch Battalion, was it duty-bound to report about the presence and activities of the BiH Army in the enclave to its higher command, to its superior command? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that seems obvious to me. That's the main responsibility of UNPROFOR in its area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was it you who read their reports or was it another service within your sector that did that?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as is customary in any army, reports are compiled within the staff ultimately after approval by the Chief of Staff and the commanders. Such reports are submitted to the next level up which summarises and in turn reports to its superior. Such a report then arrives with the corresponding sector, usually G3, the operations sector of that headquarters. And at the daily briefings the most important matters that have been brought to the attention are reported at the staff meeting, and if people are interested, they can read the reports. I didn't read the reports from each individual battalion but I did read the daily reports by the three underlying sectors within UNPROFOR, and I believe that procedure must sound very familiar to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. In addition to regular reports by the military bodies, were there also reports by intelligence services? To add to that question, let me ask you if you know whether there were intelligence services present in the demilitarised zone of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The UN did not have its own intelligence services. Let me state that from the outset. That doesn't mean that no intelligence was gathered. I know, for example, that English Special Forces were active in the area, that moreover did not report via UNPROFOR lines but via national English lines, and information that was relevant to UNPROFOR's actions arrived via our headquarters. Exactly where these people were positioned was not disclosed to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Did General Smith inform you about that? Did General Smith send you information, and as the Chief of Staff, were you informed in turn about these special services? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the services had information that was relevant to UNPROFOR's actions, then I would have been informed of such.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Would you now look at transcript page 3384, line 16 to 19, from the testimony given by Mr. Franken.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once we have the transcript on our screens, I'll read the excerpt I want us to focus on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can you tell the date of the testimony of Mr. Franken?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 30th of June. Thank you. Lines 16 to 19.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Those are the lines that I'll read out. It says: "... my superior command never asked me details about the presence of the BH Army, which should have been logical, but awhile ago I already told that you the whole intelligence cycles didn't work within UNPROFOR." Now, my question is this: Did the command of the sector, or rather, the UNPROFOR command, was it interested in knowing about the situation in the demilitarised zone and what was going on there or not? Because from what Mr. Franken says, it would appear that it was not interested. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether Mr. Franken understood the question properly at the time, but obviously within their area of responsibility, UNPROFOR troops report everything relevant about what the parties are doing in that area. And if there are incidents or if troops are found that are armed or if there are restrictions on freedom of movement, then those are all examples of things that should be reported.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we now have document 1D241 called up, please. Thank you. Since we don't have the English translation, I'm going to read it out, read paragraph 2 out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And the document is dated the 9th of June, 1995. "The weapons were handed over to UNPROFOR during the demilitarisation process. We haven't picked it up yet and divided it up in the units. We reached an agreement with the UNPROFOR command that if the aggressor carries out an infantry attack on the protected area, then at that instance, the warehouse in which UNPROFOR is storing our weapons will be open for us and the weapons will be at our disposal. "After this agreement, we sent our young guys to the weapons depot. They cleaned the weapons, separated the cleaned out barrels, and what was not working properly they separated and completed the pieces so that, in a way, we undertook preparations to take over the weapons should the need arise." And my question is the following: General, did you know that the -- there was this agreement between the UNPROFOR command and the Muslim forces in Srebrenica and that they had access to weapons, the kind of weapons described here in this warehouse? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before we hear the answer of the witness, we would like to know something about the document. You only indicated that it is dated the 9th of June, 1995. But what kind of document is it? We would like to have any identification.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you, Mr. President. This is a document written by the command of the 28th Division in Srebrenica on the 19th [as interpreted] of June, 1995, and it was sent to the command of the 285th Light Infantry Brigade in Zepa, Avdo Palic. He was subordinated to that command so that he would have this information. And then further on, although I didn't insist upon that, it says, I suggest you do the same thing we did for the whole of Bosnia, and many greetings. Much salaams or many greetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We just wanted to know the kind of document. Mr. Nicolai, please try to answer this question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's not so difficult. Previously in this hearing, I've stated that it was customary for the parties that had surrendered weapons to weapon collection points were permitted to do the maintenance. Everything in this text that they did that corresponds with the official agreements, and I am aware of agreements that in cases of dire emergencies, so if a party was attacked in a protected area, then they would be permitted to remove their weapons from the weapon collection points. And in the case of Srebrenica, at the final stage, around 10 July, the parties were offered this option, but they didn't use this option. I think that my answer is a bit more detailed than the question General Tolimir put to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I asked you this question since you deal with this question in your report, and it was a subject that was dealt with during the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, 1D242, 1D241, I should like those documents to be tendered into evidence because they speak for themselves, they show what the situation was like. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, we are in the same position as with previous documents. They will be marked for identification, and you have the choice to tender them with another witness or file a motion from -- for admission from the bar table.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 1D242 will be Exhibit D83, marked for identification. 65 ter 1D241 will be Exhibit D84, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Now may we have D67, please. Thank you. It's a document written by Mr. Delic. It says the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, General Staff of the army, and he sent it via the 1st Corps to the president of the Presidency, Mr. Izetbegovic, and he sets out all the things he undertook and did in the Srebrenica zone. And I'm going to quote the first paragraph, and we do have the English translation so you can follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: He says: "Dear Mr. President, in view of the situation of our enclaves during the preceding period, the army General Staff has undertaken a series of military activities and procedures to organise the members of the BH Army in the enclaves and prepare them for possible developments, primarily the defence of the existing free territory and planned engagement and preparations for future joint operations and planned operations." And now I'm going to read the second bullet point. It says: "17 helicopter flights were carried out in each of which a helicopter was hit." Then I'm going to quote from the fourth bullet point lower down the page, please. "In preparations for future operations, the joining up of the enclaves, we brought in four brigade commanders, two brigade chiefs of staff, and the 26th Division Chief of Staff. The division commander who was meant to go on the next helicopter flight did not return. After the final flight ended tragically, Naser remained." Now, let's look at the columns lower down and the first sentence above that. It says the attached table shows exactly what MTS was delivered, materiel and technical equipment, that is, to Srebrenica and Zepa. And then we have numbers 1 to 8 specifying the amounts of ammunition and the types of bullet supplied, hand-grenades, lasers, bombs and so on. If you look through the columns further down, you'll see that there's quite a lot of heavy weapons, mines for mortars, shells for mortars and for multiple-barrelled rocket-launchers and hand-held rocket-launchers, RPGs, et cetera. And this was signed by General Rasim Delic. My next question, if you've looked through all this, is the following -- or, rather, tell me when you finish looking through the document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw a list pass by very rapidly which -- with an extensive inventory and I wasn't able to read through it all at that pace.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Well, look at the list again and look at number 10. It says rocket-launcher, 107 millimetres. Number 10. And then look at number 11, 107-millimetre rocket-launcher, or rather, rocket. Then look at 16 and 17, 60-millimetre Commando mortars, rounds for 60-millimetre mortars, 85 of those.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've seen those, and those are both -- rockets and mortars were considered heavy arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. You can look for yourself, I'm not going to insist, but look at number 51 and 52, 82-millimetre rounds and 120-millimetre rounds delivered, and then 20-millimetre bullets for anti-aircraft machine-guns and so on. Now, my question is this: Bearing in mind that this was written on the 30th of July, 1995, and that it was sent throughout the period until the action in the enclave started, from looking at this, can you see that the Muslims, as you noted yourself, did in fact have heavy weapons which they brought in through that corridor to the area where they forbid UNPROFOR's presence, or in some other way, brought in in some other way?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'd like to check the date first. 30 July 1995 sounds exceedingly unlikely to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we see the first page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, in the text I read 30 July. If it's 30 June, that would seem more plausible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I don't know where you found the 30th, General, but this document was sent on the 13th of July, 1995, from the Main Staff via the 1st Corps command to the president, Mr. Izetbegovic, informing him what deliveries were made to Zepa and Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm reading the English text of the report of what's stated here in this courtroom. If this document is dated 13 July, then I don't know when these items listed in this report were supplied to the enclaves. But it certainly was not on 13 July because, in any case, the enclave of Srebrenica had fallen by then and Zepa was about to fall.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, for you to see this, may we have D63 called up next, please. It's about the air bridge that was constantly present between Tuzla and Zepa and bringing in weapons to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before we move to the next document, I think we should give Mr. Thayer the opportunity to address the Chamber with his response about the protective measures for the witness concerned we spoke about earlier. And then we must have a break. It should be an extended break because I was told that there's a need for some technical matters, so that we have a break now with the cross-examination. Thank you, Mr. Nicolai, again. You are allowed to leave the courtroom now because we have some procedural matters to discuss.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, are you prepared to respond to the motion of Mr. Tolimir we received in the meantime in the written official form? If you are prepared, we should move into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: As I indicated earlier, this break has to be extended by ten minutes, so that we adjourn now and resume 11.25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir -- oh, no, sorry, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President. Good afternoon. I just wanted to make one correction. I misspoke during my argument and I can do this in open session. It's at page 29 of the LiveNote, line 3, I referred to the public's right to a fair trial. Clearly, I meant to say the public's right to an open trial and that was the sole ground set forth in the response. I just wanted to clarify that for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That was my impression that you were referring to the right of the public session. Mr. Tolimir, now you have the opportunity to respond to the arguments of Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now, my legal advisor will answer the legal portion of what Mr. Thayer presented and I will deal with something that I don't think stands, in my opinion. Because he says the accused challenges the intercepts but yet refers to them. Now, I'd like to say that I did not refer to them but I didn't want to obstruct the proceedings and I took part in the work of the court normally and examined -- cross-examined the witnesses you brought in. Now, the other sentence that was added by Mr. Thayer is this: He said that the accused, while he was speaking about respect for the rulings of the Court, and he says the accused asked that the decisions under 92 bis takes on board the rulings of the Trial Chamber. I don't challenge them. So there's a big difference. And I'd like to be given a little time for comments by me, but first of all by my legal advisor. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you are aware that needs permission by the Chamber if Mr. Gajic gets the right to address legal arguments to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's why I asked with the Court's permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because we said everything in our submissions, in our motions, but since this is an -- it's not an extraordinary case. We have already dealt with it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your request is granted, and, Mr. Gajic, you get the floor, but I have a request, not to repeat the arguments we know already by your written submission. But if there's anything to add, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I precisely wanted to say what you've just said. We are not going to repeat our arguments. I'd just like to underline one point and that is this: It's not proper practice for the Prosecution to call a witness to come to The Hague while we are waiting for a Trial Chamber decision. So I think that this is a practice which is disadvantageous to the Defence. It puts us in a difficult position and I think it puts the Trial Chamber in rather a difficult position too. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The Chamber will take this into account as well. The witness should be brought in now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Nicolai, for your patience. We had some matters to discuss in your absence. Now the cross-examination will continue. Please, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: General, can you tell us whether you gave permission to your forces in Srebrenica to fight the Army of Republika Srpska within these enclaves; and if so, tell us what you were guided by and when you gave this order in terms of time? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: First I'd like to make clear that the troops did not need my direct permission to fight if they were being attacked. Their area of authority was sufficiently clear so that if they were being attacked, they were in a position to decide on their own whether they wanted to fight back. I can elaborate on that. In the period from 9 to 11 July, the situation was such that DutchBat was fully entitled to retaliate, but General Janvier, the force commander, emphasised that before deploying air force, he wanted to respond at a lower level of violence. So we brought about a situation in which if the Serb troops, and I'm referring to the blocking position, that if the position taken by DutchBat were attacked, then DutchBat had instructions to open fire on the approaching troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, may we look at the transcript of the 1st of July, page number is 3453, lines 25 -- 24 and 25, where Mr. Franken explains how he received the order from you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We have the transcript on our screens. 3453, line 25 --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation]3483 and 3484. I'd like page 3483. I don't see that. Now we have it, line 25 and 3484, line 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And I quote: "... my mandate was changed significantly the very moment the UN ordered me to defend Srebrenica, and that was the cause why I gave that green order ..." Thank you. And now my question: Did he receive specific orders from you when to enter into battle with the Army of Republika Srpska, and if so, as of what date? When to engage with the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me state first of all that this was not about staging an attack. Aside from what Major Franken alleged, he was consistently entitled in the event of self-defence to use violence, and pursuant to the UN resolutions, he was also entitled to use violence to defend the local population. That was a given. He didn't need to request specific permission for that. It was customary, however, to do so with great caution. The UN is expected to avoid becoming a party to a conflict and will therefore postpone resorting to violence as much as possible. If there's no choice, however, for self-defence or to protect the local population, they were entitled at any time to resort to violence. In this specific case, however, he received additional directives to bring about a situation where it would be clear to the entire international community that UNPROFOR was being attacked and the local population was being attacked, and what I mean here is adopting the blocking position east of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, would you show General the statement that he gave to the Prosecution on the 16th -- the 18th of November, 1996. Page 11, please, paragraph 5, lines 11 and 12. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can you please give the Court Usher the document number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D70 first, the General's statement given to the OTP, and the interview was conducted in October and the 18th of November, 1996. Page 11, lines 1 to 12 -- 11 and 12, para 5.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We can see paragraph 5 there. And the last sentence is this: "He told me to forward the message to the soldiers of the Dutch Battalion which I did."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In English it's on the following page, page 11, the first two lines. And it's the discussion between -- with General Janvier. So let's look at the first sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: "At about 1200 hours, I was told that combat air support was not given permission for and was not authorised, and the staff took three hours to make its decision." Those are the first two lines of paragraph 5.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the English it's on the previous page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've read it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Thayer is on his feet, so shall we hear him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just for the record, because, again, I don't know if this page of the statement will actually end up being tendered, we are talking about 10 July, just so we can orient ourselves down the line when we are reviewing the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, your question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Thayer. Yes, this statement is already as an exhibit and I'm quoting from paragraph 5, lines 1 and 2, and lines 11 and 12. So if Mr. Thayer wants this to go on the record, I don't mind. It can be recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And my question is this: From this, can we see that you did not receive permission for air support from Zagreb, and that you had to convey this, pass this message on to DutchBat and that you did that? That's what you say in the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What happened at that point in time, and I've stated that here, is that DutchBat had requested air support because there was an exchange of fire with approaching Serb troops and all the conditions for requesting the air support had been met, and UNPROFOR approved the request from Sarajevo and transmitted it to Zagreb because that's where the authority was to deploy air support. And over there, extensive deliberations took place as to whether or not to deploy air support, and again, it's unclear to me why it took so long, but because it took so long, dusk fell and given that the troops were extremely close together, General Janvier believed that the risk of collateral damage was too serious to deploy air support at that point. So he said, I can't approve it at this time, and he then agreed that from the next morning at 6 a.m., the airplanes would be available over the Adriatic, from where it's only a few minutes to the enclave. And depending on the situation, they would re-assess whether deploying air support was necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And my next question is based on what you've just said. For air support, once you did not get permission the first time, did you create conditions on the ground for it to be authorised a second time around? Thank you. Did you prepare the ground in anticipation of getting permission ultimately?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we had done that previously. On Sunday, 9 July, General Janvier had assigned us to order DutchBat to adopt a blocking position east of the town of Srebrenica, and the purpose was that if the troops were attacked there, it would be clear that in that situation both UNPROFOR and the local population were being threatened, and it would be more than obvious that deploying air support was justified.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you for that very sincere answer. So you did create conditions on the ground conducive to that. Now, I'm going to show you a statement you gave in the Popovic trial.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And it is P6403. Page 18481, lines 13 to 17. On e-court, it is page 27.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So Exhibit P6403, so that you can tell us again what you said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I think there is no document P6403. We don't have so many yet in this trial. Which is the right number? Mr. Thayer, can you assist us?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think the --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 6403.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Negative, Mr. President. I think the correct exhibit number is P674. If we are referring to the Popovic trial transcript of 29 November 2007 and transcript page 18481, that is P674.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Always very helpful to get your assistance. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could the witness take a look at this now, please, to see what he said in the broader context, from lines 3 to 17. And I'm just going to quote part of the discussion with General Janvier about activities to be undertaken by DutchBat. I'll give the General a few moments to read through the passage up to line 17, and when he is finished, would he let me know. It says: "Towards that time, General Janvier gave instructions that part of DutchBat should take up blocking positions, by DutchBat, to the south of Srebrenica. First of all, the object of this was to block the passage for Serb troops; and secondly, it was intended to create a situation that if they attempt to proceed, they would find themselves in the situation with no other way out but to attack." My question is as follows: Was this the kind of situation that was supposed to create conditions for calling for air support and General Janvier granting permission for air support because he asked you to pass it on to DutchBat?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: To avoid all misunderstandings, according to UN regulations, the rules for deploying air support had been met. UN Resolution 824 and 836 entitle UNPROFOR to use air support if either the local population or UNPROFOR troops are under attack, and that was the case before that point already. But General Janvier found it difficult to resort to extreme measures without violence at a lower level already and that's why he asked DutchBat to adopt a position so that it needed to be -- they would need to be attacked if the Serbs wanted to continue, and then it would be so obvious and we could start by responding to that attack with DutchBat arms. And if that was insufficient to stop the attack, then it would be overly obvious that the situation was so serious that air force needed to be deployed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 18471 is the transcript number. I misspoke, so could that be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And following on from the General's answer, my next question is this: Did that create political conditions for the use of -- for air support rather than the situation on the ground?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't believe that there were political conditions in this case, but as you know, I've made a statement previously about what was known as post air-strike guidance where force commander General Janvier advocated great caution in deploying air force and he was trying to encourage bringing about a situation. Once again, the situation was caused primarily because of the Serb armed forces situation that would eliminate any possible doubt that deployment of this extreme measure was necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now I would kindly ask you to look at D70. This is the witness's statement, page 9, paragraph 3. Line 3. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We will see page 9, paragraph 3, line 3, in a minute, and 4, and so on. Thank you. Now we can see both versions, Serbian and English, and we have paragraph 3. I'm reading from line 3 -- actually, we'll start reading from line 1: "The situation leading to the fall of Srebrenica started developing around the 6th July. On that morning, there was heavy fighting between the VRS and the ABiH. The VRS were using between five to ten tanks and heavy artillery. The shelling was mostly directed at military targets and not directly against the civilian population."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is in fact paragraph 4, not paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. In the Serbian it's paragraph number 3. It is possible that in English it's paragraph number 4. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: General, does it transpire from your statement that the civilians did not come under attack although there was fierce fighting, as you stated yourself?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is your question?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Off mike.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was the civilian population targeted during that particular attack or not?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, not yet on 6 July. What I was referring to in that context were attacks on DutchBat units.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In the statement we read that the fighting involved the BiH Army and the VRS. There's no reference to the Dutch Battalion. Did you just misspeak when you said Dutch Battalion or are you saying that the Dutch Battalion was already at the time involved in the conflict?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: By 6 July was already the first fight between DutchBat and the Bosnian Serb troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The fighting was carried out pursuant to the so-called green alert by the commander or the deputy commander, or was the fighting conducted spontaneously? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you talking about the fighting between the Bosnian Serb troops and the ABiH, or are you talking about the fighting between the Bosnian Serb troops and UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, I'm talking about you, what you stated in paragraph 3 and, as the President said, in paragraph 4 in the English version. I read out from the first four lines and you are not talking about an engagement involving the VRS and UNPROFOR, or rather, you are saying that there was heavy fighting between the VRS and the ABiH. I've taken note of your additional statement that before that the VRS opened fire on the DutchBat, as you have just stated now.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember how it figured in the course of the day. In this statement what is being referred to is fighting between the VRS and the ABiH, and what can happen there is that Dutch -- what could have happened is that DutchBat may have looked at it but not done anything about it. On that same day, there was also an attack on one of the DutchBat OPs, but I don't think that's addressed yet in this section.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, we'll come to that a bit later. We are now looking at the fifth line in the Serbian language and in the fourth line -- or, rather, the fourth paragraph in the English version, and I'm quoting: "I explained to him the day of the policy General Janvier and Smith," and you are referring to the commander of the DutchBat. "I explained that according to the actual guide-lines the use of air power was permitted for the sole Defence of UNPROFOR soldiers or in case of deliberate attacks on the civilian population. This discussion came up because some of the soldiers in the DutchBat operation posts in the south of the enclave felt threatened by the close presence of the VRS troops. Colonel Karremans wanted air presence to demonstrate to the VRS that he had the capability to use these aircraft. I did not give permission for the use of air presence ..." and so on and so forth and the end of quotation. My question is this: Since in this paragraph you said that there was no direct attack against the civilian population despite the heavy fighting between the VRS and the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, can you tell us, since you are talking about heavy fighting, does that mean that the BiH Army also had weapons from which it could open fire?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, apparently they did, and I've said earlier we never succeeded in fully disarming the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you did not approve the presence of air force and since you've said that there was no direct attack against the civilians and since you said that there was heavy fighting between the BiH Army and the VRS, was the situation later created for UNPROFOR to become target of the VRS attacks? You say in this statement that UNPROFOR was threatened by the presence of the VRS and they were not threatened by the presence of the Muslim Army. Where does the difference come from? How do you count for the difference in those two approaches?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the presence of ABiH armed forces was not so threatening to DutchBat because the ABiH had only handguns. The VRS armed forces, however, had heavy weapons, heavier weapons than DutchBat had. That's why they were somewhat fearful of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: General, you say that they did not have heavy weapons. How do you explain heavy fighting?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And while you are answering, I would like the court to produce D63 which will show you that they did have heavy weaponry that UNPROFOR was completely unaware of.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that General Tolimir has basically already provided the answer. If you are not aware that a party has heavy weapons, then you can't be afraid of that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. We have the document in front of us dated 17 February 1995, and the title is: "Final analysis of the Srebrenica and Zepa air-lift." And just awhile we saw a report from Delic to Izetbegovic as to what had arrived in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please look at the second page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm going to read the first paragraph under the word "Introduction," where it says: "Between the 27 February 1993 and the 7th May 1995, there was an air-lift from the territory of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina to meet the needs of the enclave of Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde. The main objective of introducing and maintaining the air-lift was to transport and ensure combat equipment, evacuation of the wounded, the functioning of government," and so on and so forth. And then under 2, please look at the following paragraph, the first bullet point says: "The main tasks of establishing and maintaining the air-lift were the following: Transport of weapons and military equipment, transport of combatants and passengers, transport of materiel to enable the functioning of military and civilian authorities," and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now can we go to the following page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We saw that the whole operation lasted until the month of July, 1995. You were on duty at the time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please turn to the following page of the final analysis which speaks about the existence of air-lift.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: B/C/S or English?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I would need the exact page in B/C/S as well in order to be able to comment upon what I read. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Look at the title "Losses," where it says in the last paragraph: "One helicopter was involved in an accident, the crew slightly wounded and the cargo was not damaged."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we move on to the following page. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I have a problem to follow. Perhaps it's my personal problem, but you should clearly indicate from which page and which paragraph you are quoting. I can't follow in this way, just to say, "Following page, following page," I don't know where you are at the moment. Please be a little bit more precise.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I said that the air-lift, as I read in the introduction, until the month of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please tell me which part of this document you are referring to. Which page, which paragraph? This is necessary.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We have to show the witness what happened from the time when the demilitarised zone was established and when UNPROFOR moved in what weapons arrived --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I asked you for an indication which part of this document you want to have on the screen and you are quoting from. No other explanation is wanted.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Can we now look at the table of the weapons and materiel that were air-lifted during the relevant period that I have already specified for everybody concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Tolimir, can you tell me, please, perhaps I'm not capable enough, can you tell me, please, which part of this document you referring to, exactly the page number and the paragraph number and the line number. Otherwise we are all lost. Especially the witness needs it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I read the text that I was supposed to read, that needed to be read to show how long the air-lift was present during the time when Srebrenica was a demilitarised zone, and now I'm asking for the table.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you will have realised that I stopped you. Tell me the page -- I see something on the screen, that's correct, but I want to know which page. We must have a clear transcript so that we -- later on we can follow what we are looking at. The page number, the paragraph number, and the line number again. Please do it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can the court please produce page 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could the General please look at lines 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 9 and 10, and can he also look at the totals demonstrating how many tonnes of lethal weapons were brought to Srebrenica. Thank you. We can see that a total quantity of lethal weapons was 10 tonnes.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have to see what we have in front of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just for the record, Mr. President, the table to which General Tolimir is referring appears on pages 9 to 10 of the English translation, so I think for the total that General Tolimir is referring to, which would be line number -- below line number 10, we'd have to go to the next page, which would be page 10, assuming General Nicolai has had an opportunity to review what is on page 9 in the English before him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That was exactly what I'm asking for, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now we can see it in English, segregated by months, February --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now you are in the position to put a question to the witness. Carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: General, sir, you see a table in front of you depicting an overview of all the materiel that were brought to Srebrenica during 1995, and later on we will see all the other lines after 10. You see here what lethal weapons were brought in and when from Tuzla to Srebrenica. My question is this: Were you ever informed about the arming of Muslims in Srebrenica and Zepa by means of air-lift and by means of land roads? Did your forces on the ground ever inform you about that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, despite the fact that according to me I still don't have the same page in front of me, I think you are referring to a table that you displayed earlier this morning about arms and munition that was brought in. I think I can still answer the question. First, I'd like it to be said that you are referring to an air-lift that took place from February 1993 until May 1995, so that's a very long period of which only a very small part was during my term in Sarajevo. Aside from that, the UN was certainly aware of the fact that supplies were being brought to those enclaves by air and that was the reason for an action known as Operation Deny Flight in which the NATO air forces that were available to the UN tried to block all air traffic above the Bosnia-Herzegovina territory, and that considerably reduced the number of such flights. On the other hand, we realised, and this was also clear from reports also by UNMOs that we received now and then, that we never fully succeeded in blocking that air traffic. If you know the area, and you know the area, then you know that it's very hilly and mountainous terrain, and if you are flying through the valleys in helicopter at night, then it's very difficult for fast jet planes to discover a helicopter and if necessary shoot it down there. That's why we never succeeded entirely in discontinuing this, but we certainly reduced it considerably.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I showed you the air-lift information because you asked about the weapons that Delic wrote about to Izetbegovic. Now, let's go back to your statement.
